en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Thirty, Chapter on Kiṁchanda.
9. The Sambulā Jātaka “Why do you stand alone in this mountain cave, trembling,
with your thighs pressed together?”
"You were questioned by me among those whose beauty is measured by the hand;
tell me your name and your kinsmen,
illuminating this lovely forest."
Frequented by lions and tigers—
who are you, O beautiful one?
To whom do you belong, O lady of shapely waist?
“I salute you, O Blessed One;
may there be homage to you, O giver of gifts.
“He who was the son of the King of Kāsi...”
"He is known by the wise as Sotthisena;
Sambulā is his wife—
know this, O Dānava."
I salute you, venerable sir;
I am Sambulā, may there be homage to you. You are the son of Vedehī, O Blessed One.
He lived in the forest, afflicted;
I, alone, attended upon him alone, who was overcome by illness.
And whatever I bring from the forest thicket— honey, meat,
or the burrow of a deer— that is my food.
"He surely does not heed it today.
"What will you do with the prince in the forest,
when he is so afflicted?"
“Because you have attended upon Sambula, I shall become your husband. [She replied:
“To one who is afflicted by grief and ill-clad...”
"What form do I possess?
Seek out another, O venerable sir,
who is more beautiful than I."
“Having ascended this mountain,
you shall become the most excellent among my four hundred wives.”
It fulfills all desires.
O you who possess the radiance of a star, whatever you wish for in your mind— surely it shall be so.
All that is abundant is mine; enjoy yourself today with me. If you do not accept the status of chief queen, [then...]
"You shall have sambulā prepared;
it will be enough for your breakfast,
and you shall become food for the flies."
And there was a fierce man-eater,
a hunter with matted hair and tawny skin, who,
not seeing her protector in the forest, [seized her].
She took a morsel of food to eat.
She was seized by a wicked piśāca with eyes greedy for flesh.
Having fallen under the power of the enemy,
she grieves for her husband alone:
"This suffering is not so great for me," [she thinks].
May a rakkhasa devour me,
and may my husband’s mind turn away from me.
The gods do not exist, they surely do not purify themselves;
for indeed, the guardians of the world do not exist here,
[for they would not protect] those who act with violence and are unrestrained.
"Surely there are no refuters [of this truth]!
"Among women, she is preeminent and renowned;
peaceful and composed, her brilliance is like a blazing fire."
If you command that maiden to be devoured by the Rākṣasas,
your head shall indeed split into seven pieces;
do not burn her, release her who is devoted to her husband!
And she came to the hermitage,
released from the man-eater,
like a bird that has left its nest of mud.
Like a cow that has lost her calf,
that illustrious princess lamented there in her dwelling.
Sambulā, distressed by the change of seasons and not seeing her lord in the forest,
paid homage to the recluses and brahmins.
"O you who have perfected your conduct,
not seeing the prince,
we have come to you for refuge."
I pay homage to the lions and the tigers,
and to whatever other wild animals there are in the forest,
who do not see the prince.
“We have gone for refuge to you.
Grasses, creepers, medicinal herbs,
mountains, and forests—
Not seeing the prince, [she said],
"I have gone to you for refuge.
I pay homage to her who has the luster of a blue lotus.
Seeing the night garlanded with stars,
and not seeing the prince,
she said: "I have gone to you for refuge."
I pay homage to the Ganges, the daughter of Bhagīratha,
the recipient of all rivers;
for not seeing the prince, I bow to her.
“We have gone to you for refuge.
I pay homage to Himavanta,
the best of mountain kings, that mass of rocks.
Not seeing the prince, she said,
"I have come to you for refuge.
"He has indeed arrived far too late!"
“O illustrious princess,
with whom have you been associating lately?
Who is dearer to you than I?”
“Then indeed I said this:
‘I have been seized by that enemy;
this suffering is not so painful to me.’”
Whether a rākṣasa should devour me,
or whether my noble son’s mind should become otherwise.”
“Of thieves who possess many wiles,
in whom truth is very hard to find;
the nature of women is difficult to comprehend.”
“Just as a fish that has gone into the water,
so may truth protect me,
if it will indeed protect me.”
As I do not know anyone else dearer than you,
by this utterance of truth—
“May your illness be pacified.
“Those seven hundred noble elephants, armed with weapons,
protect [me] day and night with unremitting effort.”
"And sixteen hundred archers—
what kind of beings do you see them as, O Bhaddā?
"They are adorned and have skins the color of white lotuses."
The swans and cranes behold my dispassion;
having heard their measured songs and music,
O dear one, I am no longer as I was before.
Wearing golden garments, well-proportioned,
adorned, and like celestial nymphs among humans—
O dear one, that army is beloved and its limbs are beyond reproach.
Kṣatriya maidens entice him. "If I,
dear father, were as I was before,
I would gather that husband with gleanings and support him once more in the forest."
Honor me, and do not despise me; O dear one, it would be better for me even than this,
that abundant food and drink should be set out.
A woman adorned with polished ornaments and well-decorated,
though beloved by her husband, would rather die than suffer from his malice.
It is better for her to die than that.
Even if she is poor, destitute, and without means, with only a mat for her companion,
yet dear to her husband— even if she is endowed with every excellence,
if she is not beloved, [she is of no value].
“Even this bed is better, though it be wretched, if it is shared with one who is dear.
“A woman who is beneficial to a man is very hard to find;
a husband who is both beneficial and dear to his wife is even harder to find.”
“Your wife is well-disposed toward you and virtuous, O Lord of Men;
practice the Dharma for the sake of Sambulā.
“If you were to obtain vast wealth...”
"Overcome by grief, she has met her death;
and I, Bhaddā, and these princesses—
all of us shall do as you say."
The Sambulā Jātaka, the ninth.
